test_title: RRB Group D Official Paper (Held On: 22 Dec, 2025 Shift 2)
subject: general
question: A patient is unable to move his left hand, but brain scans show no damage. Which part of the nervous system is most likely to be affected?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Peripheral nervous system**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)** consists of all the **nerves** that lie outside the **brain** and **spinal cord**. Its primary function is to connect the **Central Nervous System (CNS)** to the limbs and organs, essentially serving as a communication relay back and forth between the brain and the extremities.
 
• In the given scenario, if the **brain scans** show no damage, it indicates that the **motor cortex** and other integration centers in the **CNS** are functioning correctly. Therefore, the inability to move the **left hand** suggests an interruption in the signal path along the **peripheral nerves** that travel from the spinal cord to the muscles of the hand. ***Hence, the correct answer is the Peripheral nervous system.***
 
• The **PNS** is divided into two main parts: the **Somatic Nervous System** and the **Autonomic Nervous System**. The **Somatic Nervous System** is specifically responsible for **voluntary muscle movements** and transmitting sensory information to the **CNS**.
 
• Damage to the **Peripheral Nervous System** (often called **peripheral neuropathy**) can result in **weakness**, **numbness**, and **paralysis** in specific areas like the hands or feet, even when the **brain** remains perfectly healthy.
 
• The **PNS** includes **12 pairs of cranial nerves** and **31 pairs of spinal nerves**. These nerves carry **motor commands** to the **skeletal muscles** to initiate movement.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Central Nervous System (CNS):**
 
 
• The **CNS** comprises the **brain** and the **spinal cord**. It acts as the "control center" of the body, processing sensory information and sending out instructions.
 
• Damage to the **CNS** (such as a **stroke** or **traumatic brain injury**) would typically show up on a **brain scan** (MRI or CT), which contradicts the conditions mentioned in the question.
 
 
 
• **Autonomic Nervous System (ANS):**
 
 
• This is a component of the **PNS** that regulates **involuntary** physiologic processes, including **heart rate**, **blood pressure**, **respiration**, and **digestion**.
 
• Since moving a hand is a **voluntary action** controlled by the **Somatic Nervous System**, the **ANS** is not the primary system responsible for this specific deficit.
 
 
 
• **Parasympathetic Nervous System:**
 
 
• This is a subdivision of the **Autonomic Nervous System**. It is often referred to as the **"rest and digest"** system.
 
• It helps conserve energy by slowing the **heart rate** and increasing intestinal and gland activity. It does not control the **skeletal muscles** used to move the hand.
 
 
 
• **Sympathetic Nervous System:**
 
 
• Another branch of the **ANS**, responsible for the **"fight or flight"** response. It prepares the body for physical activity by increasing **heart rate** and diverting blood flow to **muscles**, but it does not direct the specific **voluntary motor signals** for hand movement.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Nerve Conduction:** For a muscle to contract, an **electrical impulse** must travel from the **brain**, down the **spinal cord**, through a **peripheral motor nerve**, and across the **neuromuscular junction**.
 
• **Reflex Arc:** Some movements are involuntary **reflexes** that involve only the **spinal cord** and **PNS**, bypassing the **brain** entirely. However, **voluntary movement** of the hand requires the full circuit.
 
• **Location of Injury:** Injuries to the **brachial plexus** (a network of nerves in the shoulder) or individual nerves like the **radial**, **ulnar**, or **median nerves** can cause localized hand paralysis despite a healthy **brain**.
